Q: How do I automatically approve "low risk" Github Copilot commands in VS Code? A:

Yes. In recent versions of VS Code, the closest built-in option is Assisted permissions.

You can enable it with:

"chat.assistedPermissions.enabled": true

Then select Assisted permissions from the permissions menu in the Chat/Agent view. VS Code uses an AI-based judge to decide whether a tool call can be automatically approved; calls it doesn't approve will still require confirmation.

The green/red risk assessment shown for commands is separate. chat.tools.riskAssessment.enabled only controls whether that risk assessment is displayed—it does not let you configure an automatic approval threshold based on the risk color.

If you want deterministic control instead, you can use chat.tools.terminal.autoApprove to explicitly allow specific commands or patterns.

I would avoid enabling global auto-approval just for this use case, since that effectively removes the approval safeguard rather than selectively approving lower-risk commands.

Q: CodeIgniter's where() method is excluded from built query when called after get() A:

Use this:

$this->db->get()->custom_row_object(0, 'Your_Model');

The code above is mentioned by the codeigniter user guide. The best about this is no need to loop foreach where you can get very specific row value.

Q: How should applications written in C access the cursor theme under Wayland? A:

The cursor shape wayland protocol allows you to request a cursor, by enumerator, from the compositor which should do what you want.

https://wayland.app/protocols/cursor-shape-v1

Q: Racing wheel. Force FeedBack. Simulation of real behavior A:

Force feedback in racing wheels usually works via USB Physical Interface Device (PID) Specification.

https://www.usb.org/document-library/device-class-definition-pid-10

The spec itself was modelled after Microsoft DirectInput (now deprecated) and its docs may be handy:

https://learn.microsoft.com/previous-versions/windows/desktop/ee417563(v=vs.85)

Q: Avoid overwriting existing columns in data.table functions A:

All this painful name-checking and metaprogramming is only necessary if we insist on working within the original data.table, with the unknown/irrelevant columns in scope.

Solution:

Instead, put the input column in a new table, compute the new columns there, then fix their names in one line before combining with the original.

This insulates the original columns from overwriting but remains copyless, because we can add the new columns back by reference, and moreover we only need a shallow copy of the input column (since it only needs to be read, not modified).

f <- function(x, input_col_name) {
  
  # (1) shallow-copy the input column into a new data.table
  dt <- setDT(list(input = x[[input_col_name]]))
  
  # (2) compute new columns, e.g
  dt[, mpg := input + 4][, Petal.Length := mpg / sum(mpg)][, flipper_len := letters[1:.N]]
  
  # (3) fix their names
  dt[, input := NULL]
  setnames(dt, tail(make.unique(c(names(x), names(dt))), ncol(dt)))
  
  # (4) "plonk" them by reference into the target table
  x[, (names(dt)) := dt]
  
}

(There are variants of (4) such as using copy(x)[<...>] or just returning dt[] to the caller - whatever is required. The point is that there is no use of language constructs at all, and no additional deep copies made.)

Illustrations:

DT1 <- as.data.table(mtcars[1:3,1:4], keep.rownames="model")
DT2 <- as.data.table(iris[1:3,2:3])
DT3 <- as.data.table(penguins[1:3,3:5])

f(DT1, "disp")
DT1
#>            model   mpg   cyl  disp    hp mpg.1 Petal.Length flipper_len
#>           <char> <num> <num> <num> <num> <num>        <num>      <char>
#> 1:     Mazda RX4  21.0     6   160   110   164    0.3727273           a
#> 2: Mazda RX4 Wag  21.0     6   160   110   164    0.3727273           b
#> 3:    Datsun 710  22.8     4   108    93   112    0.2545455           c

f(DT2, "Sepal.Width")
DT2
#>    Sepal.Width Petal.Length   mpg Petal.Length.1 flipper_len
#>          <num>        <num> <num>          <num>      <char>
#> 1:         3.5          1.4   7.5      0.3456221           a
#> 2:         3.0          1.4   7.0      0.3225806           b
#> 3:         3.2          1.3   7.2      0.3317972           c

f(DT3, "bill_len")
DT3
#>    bill_len bill_dep flipper_len   mpg Petal.Length flipper_len.1
#>       <num>    <num>       <int> <num>        <num>        <char>
#> 1:     39.1     18.7         181  43.1    0.3292590             a
#> 2:     39.5     17.4         186  43.5    0.3323147             b
#> 3:     40.3     18.0         195  44.3    0.3384263             c
